newsitem.title: UK: CBI opposes more rigid corporate governance rules.
newsitem.headline: CBI opposes more rigid corporate governance rules.

text.p: The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) on Monday attacked calls to slap rigid rules on how companies are managed, saying the current, flexible approach reflects the fact that "all companies are different".

In a speech to the CBI's annual conference B.A.T Industries chief executive Martin Broughton, who heads the CBI's company affairs committee, said the London Stock Exchange had implemented the recommendations of the Greenbury and Cadbury committees on corporate governance "in a non-prescriptive way".

"This flexible approach could be undermined by the growing number of self-appointed guardians with a box-ticking mentality who seek to require companies to comply with every provision of the (Greenbury and Cadbury) codes, regardless of a company's circumstances," he said. "We must avoid overcodification."

David Barnes, chief executive of Britain's third-biggest drugs company Zeneca Group, told the conference there was a danger of the codes becoming "tightly-drawn prescriptive rules and statutes subject to intense and formal audit, where even minor non-compliance can result in a sanction as great as delisting on the London Stock Exchange".
Both Barnes and Broughton attacked the idea of importing two-tier board structures to Britain along the lines of those that operate in countries like Germany and the Netherlands.
Broughton said the current unitary board and system of executive and non-executive directors "is quite simply the system that suits British companies best".
Zeneca's Barnes added that there is "no evidence of which I am aware that two-tier boards deliver in practice superior corporate governance".
